sections.title: The group and its boundary
sections.guidance:
Name the group precisely enough that every later section has a referent: who is a member, a user, an outsider; what is shared; and whether one person's use reduces another's (subtractable) or not. Durable commons have clear boundaries (`09` ch 3; Cox et al. 2010) [E], but open-source projects, platforms and knowledge commons are open by design at the outer layer. The founding mistake is answering "open or closed" for the whole group instead of layer by layer (`primer §6, §8`). Facts about the group are [E: own data]; every open/closed decision that is a design choice is [H], and a boundary chosen on principle is [V]. Revise this section at v4, once s9 and s10 have shown which boundary the institution and the seeding plan actually need.

**What good looks like:** three layers (core, regulars, periphery) each with a membership rule; a resource table marking subtractable versus non-subtractable; the scarce resource named in one sentence; churn and newcomer ratio; the open/closed answer per layer, tagged [H] where it is a choice.

**Common failures:** "the community" with no membership rule; treating code or docs as the scarce resource when it is attention; deciding openness once for the whole group.
prompts: Who says "I am part of this", and whom does the core say is part of it? Where do the two lists differ?
Which resources are used up by use (review time, moderator time, a channel's signal) and which are not (docs, code, reputation)?
What is churn per quarter, and how many newcomers arrive per experienced member?
Which boundary is open now that a later section will want to close, and which is closed that should open?

sections.title: Diagnosis: the games being played
sections.guidance:
Draw the two or three central interactions before proposing anything (law 1): players, options, payoffs as members construe them, order, information. Then ask the one test: does a member gain by defecting when everyone else cooperates? Yes means a dilemma, and the fix set is payoffs, repetition, detection and sanctions; no means a stag hunt, and the fix set is assurance, correlation and pledges (`04` ch 4, 10; `07` ch 1; ledger rule 13) [E for the theorems]. Your group's classification is always [H], before and after the defection question is answered with its own payoffs. This section governs assurance and talk versus enforcement (t07). The founding mistake is a stag-hunt fix for a dilemma, or sanctions for a stag hunt, where they signal distrust and raise the lone cooperator's cost. Check one existing sanction for credibility and separation (`04` ch 8, 9), and ask whether a "defector" is a one-shot player rather than a type.

**What good looks like:** a payoff matrix or two-curve sketch per interaction; the defection question answered in one sentence; the shape tagged [H]; the fix set listed; at least one v0 fix marked "withdrawn: wrong shape".

**Common failures:** proposing fixes before drawing the game; tagging the shape [E]; explaining one-shot players as bad types.
prompts: What does the cooperator get when all others defect, and the defector when all others cooperate?
Is the interaction repeated with the same people, and how fast is defection detected?
Which existing threat would its enforcer actually carry out, and does it separate careful from careless members?
If you reclassified the main interaction, which v0 fix would you withdraw?

sections.title: The collective brain
sections.guidance:
Map the actual learning network, never the org chart: whom newcomers watch, whom they ask, and which processes live in one head. Humans copy prestigious and successful models more than they follow explanations (`01` ch 3–5, 8) [E]; norm adherence spreads by modelling, whereas skills with hidden structure need explicit teaching (`02` ch 8; Morgan et al. 2015, one study, N = 184; ledger rule 8). This section governs copying versus teaching (t01). The founding mistake is "just document it" for a norm, or "just model it" for a skill. Name the single points of failure, the prestigious members and whether they model the target behaviour, and at least one place where a leader's costly actions contradict the stated norm: credibility-enhancing displays cut both ways (`01` ch 8). Claims about who copies whom in your group are [H] until observed.

**What good looks like:** a learning-network sketch; a single-point-of-failure list; a prestige list with a "models the target?" column; one behaviour predicted to change if a prestigious member adopts it, and one that will not change however well it is explained.

**Common failures:** mapping reporting lines; a documentation fix for a modelling problem; ignoring what the most-copied member actually does.
prompts: When someone new needs to learn how things are done, whom do they watch and whom do they ask?
Which critical process lives in one head, and what happens when that person leaves?
Which prestigious member visibly does the opposite of the stated norm?
Which target behaviours are norms (model them) and which are skills with hidden structure (teach them)?

sections.title: Situational audit and folk-psychology check
sections.guidance:
For every v0 failure, write the situational alternative to the dispositional story: workload, ambiguity, visibility, ownership, deliberation design (`03` ch 1, 5, 12; the attribution error; loafing under low identifiability) [E for the mechanisms; H that they explain your case]. This section governs dispositions versus structure (t14). The founding mistake is "the people are the problem", closely followed by a lever from the failed-replication list (ego depletion, priming, power posing, watching eyes, Stanford Prison, groupthink as a syndrome, IAT training; ledger rule 20). Strike those levers through with the reason; the strike-through is the learning. Record the current descriptive and injunctive signals per target behaviour and whether they agree, and never advertise low adoption (`03` ch 9; Schultz et al. 2007; rule 24; law 5).

**What good looks like:** a two-column table per failure (v0 story, situational alternative); a signal audit with an "agree?" column; struck levers with reasons; one structural change with a predicted effect size in words.

**Common failures:** character explanations left standing; a "we're drowning, please help" message that advertises the low rate; a lever that rests on a failed finding.
prompts: For each "they don't care" line, what would the same behaviour look like from someone who cared but faced this workload, ambiguity and visibility?
What tells a member what most people here do, and what is approved? Do the two signals agree?
Which v0 lever rests on a failed finding, and what replaces it?
Where is effort unidentifiable, and what one change would make it identifiable?

sections.title: Threshold and tipping map
sections.guidance:
Decide whether the target behaviour is contingent on how many others do it, and where the group sits relative to the crossing. Mild individual contingency produces two stable states, low and high, with an unstable tipping point between them (`05` ch 3, 7; `10` ch 17) [E for the model]; the scarce resource is low-threshold actors, never "influencers" (ledger rule 18). This is tension t04 in population form. The founding mistake is ignoring arithmetic: mentors per mentee, reviewers per review, hours per unit of work. Sketch the two curves and mark the current state. Estimate the minimum viable coalition k as [H]. State one accounting identity v0 ignored (`05` ch 2). Separate conventions, which are self-enforcing, from norms that need a rule.

**What good looks like:** a two-curve sketch with the group's position marked; k with reasoning and the pilot that tests it; one identity in numbers; the convention/rule split; a sentence on what happens if the coalition falls one short.

**Common failures:** a plan with no number, so no way to know it succeeded; recruiting the most visible member instead of the lowest-threshold one; a pilot whose game differs from the game at scale.
prompts: If a third of the group did it, would you? If two-thirds? Whose threshold is lower than yours?
Units of work per week divided by people willing and able: does the plan add up?
What is the smallest coalition that could run a pilot where the game is the same as at scale?
Which norms survive if nobody is watching (conventions) and which collapse (need a rule)?

sections.title: Population of types and fairness baseline
sections.guidance:
State the type mix in words, what conditional cooperators can see of others' contributions, and the group's own fairness reference point. Lab populations are roughly a third self-interested and about half conditional cooperators (Camerer's summary, background; direction only) [E as direction; H for your mix]; fairness is cue- and expectation-dependent, not a fixed taste (ledger rule 9). This section governs t05 and t11. The founding mistake is explaining by selfishness what is strategic uncertainty among conditional cooperators who cannot see each other. Find any weak-link process and its size: pairs reach the top, groups of 14–16 collapsed within about ten rounds (`06` ch 7; Van Huyck et al. 1990). Pick the amendment that explains the v0 failure: social preferences, limited reasoning, or learning and history.

**What good looks like:** the type mix with the visibility gap named; the reference point and comparison group; weak-link processes with their sizes; the amendment defended in a sentence; a prediction for what changes when contributions become visible.

**Common failures:** quoting an ultimatum-game figure as your group's; calling one-shot newcomers selfish; a committee where a pair would do.
prompts: Of the under-contributors, how many would contribute if they could see others doing so?
What allocation do members compare, and against whom?
Which process aggregates by the minimum, and how many people are in it?
What would members read as a broken promise, and has one occurred?

sections.title: Equilibrium selection plan
sections.guidance:
For the main stag hunt, plan how to reach the payoff-dominant state. Risk dominance wins under random mixing, best-response updating, large groups and no communication; payoff dominance is reachable through correlation: small stable groups, success-visible imitation, public pledges, gradual growth from a core, and a lower cost of being the lone cooperator (`07` ch 1, 3; `06` ch 7; Weber 2006, one lab lineage; ledger rule 2) [E for the mechanisms; H for the regime and rate here]. Sweetening the joint payoff is the weakest lever (law 3). The founding mistake is a big-bang rollout to a mixed audience with a bonus attached. State the regime, choose the cheapest correlation device (location, signal, or partner choice), and remember that local interaction helps only under success-copying (rules 3, 36). Cheap talk roughly doubles lab cooperation and decays without sanctions or repetition where defection dominates (rule 12; law 6).

**What good looks like:** regime named; the watershed in words; the device chosen and costed; the lone cooperator's loss today and the change that halves it; a pacing rate from a named core; a dated prediction of pledge decay.

**Common failures:** money as the first lever; rollout to everyone at once; a pledge round with nothing to sustain it.
prompts: Who interacts with whom, how often does it change, and is success visible when it happens?
What is the cheapest way to make cooperators meet cooperators more than chance?
What does the lone cooperator lose today, and what change halves it?
From which core, at what rate per period, does the rollout grow?

sections.title: Norm register
sections.guidance:
Classify each "norm" by the expectations that sustain it: descriptive norm, convention, social norm (conditional on empirical and normative expectations, and able to exist while widely violated), or moral norm (`08` ch 1; ledger rule 11) [E for the taxonomy and method; H for every result in your group]. Assume every norm is conditional until it survives a collapse of expectations (rule 10). This section governs broadcasting the majority versus building normative expectations (t10). The founding mistake is a values campaign aimed at pluralistic ignorance, or a "most people do it" message where nobody does (`primer §1`). Run the four-question battery per behaviour in the reference network, not the org chart: what you do, what most of them do, what they think you should do, what happens to a deviator, plus a sanction item. Empirical expectations tend to dominate normative ones (Bicchieri & Xiao 2009, lab). Measure the perceived-versus-actual gap (Tankard & Paluck 2016). Record cues as [H] for any cue-to-norm mapping (rule 37); name trendsetters by nomination.

**What good looks like:** at least three N-nn rows, each classified, with expectations, gap direction, signals, cues and trendsetters; one expectation measured before v3; a prediction of which norm collapses if one visible member deviates.

**Common failures:** surveying the org chart; a dead rule mistaken for pluralistic ignorance; cues asserted as evidence.
prompts: For each norm: what do members do, think others do, think others expect, and expect to happen to a deviator? Where does the pattern show pluralistic ignorance?
Whose opinion would a member actually notice? That is the reference network.
What template, label or bot message activates the norm at the moment of action?
Which norm collapses if one visible member deviates?

sections.title: Institutional design
sections.guidance:
Run Ostrom's eight principles as a diagnostic checklist, not a recipe: boundaries, congruence, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognition, nesting (`09` ch 3; Cox et al. 2010, 91 studies, with publication-bias and structure-not-process caveats; rule 29) [E for the regularity; H for each rule here; V for legitimacy choices]. Flag scope for digital commons. This section governs designed versus self-governed rules (t06) and incentives versus norm-based motivation (t12). The founding mistake is a rule announced by the wrong person with a first sanction so severe nobody applies it. First sanctions are small and graduated; monitoring is a by-product of use (rule 30; law 9). Write the ladder with a trigger per rung (`primer §2`). Anti-social punishment is real, so pilot before opening peer sanctions (Herrmann et al. 2008); fines can turn a norm into a price (Gneezy & Rustichini 2000). Elected sanctioners beat appointed ones with identical powers (Baldassarri & Grossman 2011; `primer §3`). State each rule's legitimacy source, the four procedural-justice components, the rule level of each fix, who has standing to change it (`09` ch 2), and the external backstop.

**What good looks like:** eight rows with scope notes; a ladder with triggers; the by-product monitoring channel; forum and appeal; legitimacy per rule; backstop; the first cheap change that produces both information and standing.

**Common failures:** close-or-nothing sanctions; a bounty where credit would do; nobody with standing to change the rule.
prompts: For each principle: present, absent, or not applicable, with a scope note?
Who can sanction whom, at what cost to themselves, with what appeal?
What is the first, smallest sanction, and how many members climbed each rung last quarter?
Who decided the rules, and can members show where their input changed them?
Which v0 fix was an operational rule, and who has standing to change it?

sections.title: Network map and seeding plan
sections.guidance:
Sketch clusters and bridges, estimate the adoption threshold q, and place the seed. A node adopts when at least q = b/(a+b) of its neighbours have; a cluster of density above 1 − q blocks a cascade from outside and protects one adopted inside (`10` ch 19, theorem; rule 3) [E for the theorem; H for your q and map]. Information crosses one weak tie; costly behaviour needs several adopting neighbours and wide bridges (rule 34). This section governs closure versus bridges (t09). The founding mistake is announcing a costly norm across weak ties and expecting adoption. Name the copying kind and its fix: an informational cascade (collect private signals first), a network effect (cross the tipping point), or coordination on a graph (lower q or seed inside clusters; rule 19). Quote only the structural weak-tie claim (rule 33); assume selection over influence when clusters look alike (rule 35); seed inside clusters and grow slowly (law 8).

**What good looks like:** a map with bridge holders named; q with reasoning; the blocking cluster and the protecting one; the seed placed inside a cluster; the copying kind and its fix; which sub-group never adopts through current bridges.

**Common failures:** a broadcast to the whole network; one bridge holder carrying the whole rollout; homophily read as influence.
prompts: Which sub-groups talk mostly to themselves, who holds the ties between them, and how many such ties are there?
How many adopting neighbours does a typical member need before adopting?
Which cluster blocks the norm, and which protects it once adopted?
Is convergence here a cascade, a network effect, or coordination on a graph, and what does that imply for the fix?

sections.title: The signal and the BPC statement
sections.guidance:
Name the public signal per coordination problem and check its visibility. Nash equilibrium is a social achievement: aligned conjectures come from a public signal, a choreographer (`11` ch 7; Aumann & Brandenburger 1995; rule 31) [E for the mechanism; H for what serves as the signal here]. Run the two-part norm test on the main norm: epistemic (can everyone say what it requires of them and of others) and motivational (does anyone gain by deviating, and is there a cheap sanction). Write one BPC line: beliefs about each other, preferences including status and fairness, constraints; it is bookkeeping, not explanation. Then audit which of the four layers v0 addressed: the stability test, selection absent intervention, the signal, and the expectations inside agents (rule 1). This section governs t03. The founding mistake is a vague value ("be welcoming") in place of a specific signal (law 11).

**What good looks like:** a signal per problem with who can and cannot see it; pass/fail on each half of the norm test with the fix for each failure; a one-line BPC; a four-layer audit of v0; a prediction of what each layer alone would move.

**Common failures:** a document mistaken for a choreographer; a norm nobody can state in one sentence; fixes that touch layer three only.
prompts: What one public thing tells everyone what to do and what others will do? Who cannot see it?
Can a newcomer state the main norm's requirement in one sentence?
Who gains by deviating while others comply, and what cheap sanction meets them?
Which layer did v0 touch, and which layer alone would move behaviour here?

sections.title: Open hypotheses register
sections.guidance:
Every [H] in s1–s11 gets a row here. This register is the brief's experimental design; without it, hypotheses are opinions with a label. "Why H not E" names the missing step: a lab result not observed in this group, a classification not checked against the group's own payoffs, or a parameter the sources leave open. "Decision rule" says what result keeps, revises or abandons the row, written before the test. Every row needs a balancing measure, because an intervention that is wrong does harm somewhere, and the register is where you commit to seeing it. Statuses are updated each version, and a row that resolves moves to "supported here" with date and evidence, never to a general [E].

**Row fields:** Id (H-nn, never reused), Hypothesis, Section, Why H not E, Test, Prediction, Practical measure, Balancing measure, Decision rule, Review date, Status.

**What good looks like:** every column filled; no row without a balancing measure; no duplicate hypotheses; the riskiest bets scheduled first; every row also appearing as an s14 line.

**Common failures:** an [H] in the body with no row; a prediction with no direction or size; "we'll see how it goes" in place of a decision rule.
prompts: Have you found every [H] in s1–s11 and given it a row?
What would you see in ninety days if the hypothesis is true, and if it is false?
What cheap observation moves this toward E for this group, or kills it?
What harm would the intervention cause if the row is wrong, and how would you see it?

sections.title: Value commitments register
sections.guidance:
Every [V] in the brief gets a row of the form "We choose X over Y". A value with no reasonable dissenter is a platitude; one with no cost is a description. The point is not to defend values with evidence but to hold them knowingly, see what they cost, and stop values being laundered as findings (law 12). Evidence can inform a commitment by revealing its consequences; it cannot settle it. Apply `primer §10` to each intervention the value licenses: is it reflective or automatic, disclosed or not; who consented; who bears the cost when it misfires; what is the exit. Name the real dissenter and their strongest argument, not a straw man. At least two capstone challenges will attack rows here.

**Row fields:** Id (V-nn), Commitment ("We choose X over Y"), Section, Who reasonably disagrees and their best argument, Cost, Evidence that informs it, Conflicts with, Owner and review.

**What good looks like:** four to eight rows, each with a named dissenter and a cost; no row that restates evidence; the conflicts column non-empty for at least two rows; an owner who can reopen each commitment.

**Common failures:** "everyone agrees contributors matter"; a value tagged [E] because a source approves; an undisclosed nudge with no row.
prompts: What are we optimising for, and what are we knowingly giving up?
Who would object, and what is the strongest version of their objection?
Which interventions sit in the automatic-and-undisclosed quadrant, and who consented?
Who can change this rule, and who can leave at what cost?

sections.title: Measurement plan and ninety-day predictions
sections.guidance:
Convert the registers into three measures per intervention: the practical measure (the behaviour or expectation expected to move, from logs or the battery), the predicted value (direction and size in words, or a number from your own baseline, with a date), and the balancing measure (what would show harm: newcomer rejection, reviewer churn, anti-social sanctioning, the boomerang, load shifting onto the already loaded). Surveys measure beliefs and logs measure behaviour; report both, because the mismatch is diagnostic (`primer §1`). Then re-measure and revise: if both moved, scale gradually; if behaviour only, the change rides on observation and will decay; if expectations only, the game is unstable at layer one, so return to s2 (`unified-model` §4). Every s12 row must appear here, and the main hypothesis must carry an abandonment condition.

**Row fields:** Intervention (id), Practical measure, Baseline (own data, date), Predicted at day 90, Balancing measure, Harm threshold, Abandon if, Owner, Cadence.

**What good looks like:** three dated predictions; a balancing measure per intervention; an abandonment condition for the main hypothesis that says what it would mean about the s2 shape; the re-measurement date.

**Common failures:** a measure the intervention can satisfy without behaviour changing; no baseline; no number that would make you stop.
prompts: What is the first cheap change that produces both information and standing?
For each intervention, what number do you expect on day 90, and what number makes you stop?
What could go up that you would not want, and are you logging it?
Which measure can the intervention satisfy without the behaviour changing, and what replaces it?
